property_summary: For any caller who is the current owner and any address newOwner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner getter equals the provided newOwner; the mutant that assigns msg.sender instead breaks this because owner becomes the caller instead of newOwner for some inputs.

After any call to transferOwnership(newOwner) made by the current owner, the contract's owner must equal the provided newOwner (the reference preserves the explicitly passed newOwner); the mutant that writes tx.origin instead can break this by setting owner to tx.origin instead of the supplied address.

For any caller who is the current owner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner() equals the provided newOwner; the mutant that assigns tx.origin instead will set owner to tx.origin for some fuzzed newOwner (when tx.origin != newOwner), breaking this rule.
For any address caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in owner() == newOwner; the mutant that assigns tx.origin instead breaks this when tx.origin != newOwner.

Invariant: only the current owner can successfully call transferOwnership to change owner; the mutant inverts the check so non-owners can call it, breaking this rule for inputs where caller == original owner and newOwner is any address.

For any caller A and target newOwner B, if A is the current owner then transferOwnership(A->B) succeeds and sets owner to B; the mutant inverts the check so a call from the current owner will be rejected and/or leave owner unchanged, so some inputs (caller == current owner) distinguish them.

For any caller addr and any newOwner addr2, a call to transferOwnership by the current owner must succeed (not revert) and set owner to the supplied newOwner; the mutant inverts the require so an original-owner caller will be rejected (or will not update owner) for some inputs, breaking this rule.

For all callers, calling transferOwnership only changes C.owner when the caller is the current owner (reference enforces this); the mutant removes the check so a non-owner can change owner for some input caller addresses, violating the rule.

For every caller address, calling owned() on the correct contract C does not change the public owner variable (only transferOwnership can), whereas the mutant that inverts the onlyOwner check allows non-owners to call owned() and thus can change owner-observable behaviour (owned() execution differs), so the rule is: calling owned() never succeeds in changing owner for any caller — reference preserves owner unchanged, mutant allows some caller to execute owned() when they are not owner and thus can alter observable state.

Invariant: only the contract owner can successfully call owned(), so after any call to owned() the owner state variable remains unchanged; the mutant removes the onlyOwner check allowing non-owners to call owned() which can change/observe owner, violating this invariant for some caller addresses.

For every caller address, calling owned() on the correct contract never changes the public owner (onlyOwner prevents non-owners from executing owned), but the mutant that removes the check allows some caller to call owned() and thereby observe a different owner value — so the invariant is that owner remains equal to the initially set owner after any call to owned(); the mutant can violate this for some caller address.

For all caller addresses, calling owned() on the correct contract either reverts for non-owners (preventing execution) or leaves owner unchanged; the mutant removes the onlyOwner guard so some caller can execute owned() successfully and (via a malicious caller that is also a contract) change observable behavior of owner/getter — thus the property is that non-owner callers cannot change owner via owned() and owner() remains equal to the initially set owner after any call by any caller.
